title: Position: Evaluation of ECG Representations Must Be Fixed
claim: Current benchmarks use narrow tasks and point estimates that suggest a clear winner; broader tasks and rigorous protocols show no method prevails.
layout: Left-to-right flow splitting into 2 stacked branches, each ending in a result plot
description: A left-to-right flow diagram. On the far left, a red 12-lead ECG trace labeled '12L ECG' leads by an arrow to a neural network icon labeled 'Pre-trained Encoder', then to a pink vertical 'Embedding' box. The arrow splits into two stacked teal rounded panels. Top panel, 'a) Current Evaluation', holds a Tasks box (arrhythmia + waveform) and a Protocol box (macro-AUROC, point estimates, tasks with insufficient support). Bottom panel, 'b) Proposed Evaluation', holds a longer Tasks list (arrhythmia, structural disease, hemodynamics, patient forecasting) and a Protocol list (task-specific AUCs, uncertainty, standard baseline, excluding low-support tasks). Each panel has an arrow to a light-blue result box. The top box shows a staircase of ranked point-estimate bars. The bottom box shows overlapping boxplots with error bars crossing a random-baseline band.
caption: Overview of the evaluation pipeline for 12-lead ECG representations. (a) Current practice focuses on arrhythmia/waveform tasks and macro-AUROC point estimates, which can produce misleading method rankings. (b) We propose a broader set of clinically relevant tasks and evaluation best-practices that more reliably assess methods. We find that no method consistently prevails and for many tasks, many methods overlap with the baseline of a randomly initialized encoder.
abstract: This position paper argues that current benchmarking practice in 12-lead ECG representation learning must be fixed to ensure progress is reliable and aligned with clinically meaningful objectives. The field has largely converged on three public multi-label benchmarks (PTB-XL, CPSC2018, CSN) dominated by arrhythmia and waveform-morphology labels, even though the ECG is known to encode substantially broader clinical information. We argue that downstream evaluation should expand to include an assessment of structural heart disease and patient-level forecasting, in addition to other evolving ECG-related endpoints, as relevant clinical targets. Next, we outline evaluation best practices for multi-label, imbalanced settings, and show that when they are applied, the literature's current conclusion about which representations perform best is altered. Furthermore, we demonstrate the surprising result that a randomly initialized encoder with linear evaluation matches state-of-the-art pre-training on many tasks. This motivates the use of a random encoder as a reasonable baseline model. We substantiate our observations with an empirical evaluation of five representative ECG pre-training approaches across six evaluation settings: the three standard benchmarks, a structural disease dataset, hemodynamic inference, and patient forecasting.
